news.2026-10-24-france-taux-5-pourcent-p: France borrows at more than 5% for the first time since 2002
The rate at which the French state borrows over ten years has crossed 5%, a level not seen for twenty-four years. The gap with Germany is the widest since 2011.
On 22 October, the yield on French ten-year bonds rose above 5% for the first time since 2002, level with the United States at around 5.1% [1][2].

The gap with Germany, the eurozone's best performer, exceeded 160 basis points, its highest since November 2011; on 23 October France borrowed at about 5.05% against 3.33% for Germany, a gap of 1.72 points [1][3].

The strain comes ahead of the European Central Bank's decision: it has raised rates twice this year, to 2.5%, and eurozone inflation reached 3.8% in September. Unions are calling for a large mobilisation on 5 November [4].
The first sentence to remember: lending to France now costs as much as lending to the United States, which will weigh on the state budget for years [1].

When investors demand more interest to lend to a country, it is because they worry about its finances or its political stability. The sources cite concern over the budget and social unrest [2][4]. The more debt costs, the more interest the state must pay, and the less it has left for schools, hospitals or roads.
State borrowing rates are a benchmark for banks: if France borrows at a higher rate, mortgages and business loans tend to follow.

news.2026-10-24-bresil-chine-moitie-petr: When Hormuz closed, China bought half of Brazil's oil
Deprived of part of the Gulf's oil by the war in Iran, China turned to Brazil: its purchases of Brazilian crude hit a record, as did trade between the two countries.
According to Brazil-China Business Council data for January-September, China took half of all the crude Brazil exported, nearly seven times the share of India, the second-largest buyer [1][2].
Brazilian oil sales to China jumped 49% to $21.8 billion: 27% more volume and prices up 16.8% [1].
Trade between the two countries hit a record $143 billion in nine months (142 according to other outlets citing the same data). The rise is slowing now that Gulf tankers are sailing again [1][2][3].
The first sentence to remember: the closure of a strait in the Middle East enriched a South American country, because buyers looked for oil elsewhere [1].

The future remains open: if Iran attacks ships in the strait again, China could turn to Brazil once more [3]. The country is also in the middle of a campaign: the presidential runoff takes place on Sunday 25 October [4].
The oil China no longer buys from the Gulf is paid for more dearly by others. Oil routes are being redrawn, and it eventually shows up in the price of a tank of fuel.

news.2026-10-24-fidji-drones-de-mer-aust: Australia gives Fiji sea drones to watch over its ocean
Canberra will give Fiji's military crewless boats that stay at sea for months. Stated aim: tracking drug trafficking in the Pacific.
Australia will give Fiji's military "Bluebottle" surface drones, as part of the Waqa Moana partnership, a Pacific-led effort against organised crime and drug trafficking [1][2].
These crewless vessels run on renewable energy and can stay at sea for more than 180 days; they are due to arrive in Fiji in early 2027 [1][2].

The announcement was repeated in Suva on 23 October by Australia's High Commissioner, Peter Roberts, alongside Fiji's Defence Minister, Pio Tikoduadua [3]. In 2025, the New Zealand navy had already patrolled Fiji's waters with two Bluebottles for three months [4].
The first sentence to remember: a small archipelago gets eyes on a huge ocean thanks to crewless boats donated by a neighbour [1].
Pacific countries have very large sea areas but few means to monitor them. The drones donated by Australia also strengthen its influence in a region where the big powers compete for alliances [2].
Drug and trade routes also cross the Pacific; watching them is expensive, and these drones show how countries are now going about it.

news.2026-10-24-jordanie-fusillade-eglis: Jordan: gunmen open fire in a church in the south, at least seven dead
A shooting hit a church in Karak governorate during a funeral. The toll is at least seven dead and 34 wounded.
On 23 October, gunmen opened fire in a church in Karak governorate, in southern Jordan, during a funeral: at least seven people died and 34 were wounded [1].
Saudi Arabia condemned a "cowardly" attack on the church [2].
The sources consulted do not yet say who is behind the attack or why [1][2].
The first sentence to remember: a country seen as an island of calm in a region at war has just been hit on its own soil [1].

For Jordan's economy, security matters: the safer a country looks, the more tourists and investors come. Investigators have not yet said who was responsible, so it is too early to measure the consequences [1][2].
If you are planning a trip to the Middle East, check the French foreign ministry's travel advice before booking.

news.2026-10-24-ukraine-starshield-satel: Ukraine: after the Starshield cut-off, Kyiv wants its own satellite network
Since the American military network Starshield was restricted, the Ukrainian army knows it depends on a tool it does not control. Kyiv is preparing an independent system.
Starshield, the military version of Starlink, has been shared with Ukraine by the Pentagon since 2024, at a cost of billions of dollars to it [1][2].

In mid-October, the connection was restricted for systems moving above a certain speed, which hit drones and air defence around Kyiv. A source at Ukraine's Defence Ministry says it has been restored, but Volodymyr Zelensky says it has not been fully restored [2][3].

Volodymyr Zelensky blames Washington, Elon Musk replies that Starshield belongs to the US government, and Donald Trump denies having intervened. Senators are calling for an investigation by the Pentagon's inspector general. On 23 October, Ukraine announced it was preparing an independent satellite system [1][2][3].
The first sentence to remember: Ukraine has discovered that part of its defence depends on a network whose off switch is in other hands [3].

The more a country depends on foreign technology to defend itself, the more its allies can weigh on it. That is what pushes Kyiv to want its own satellites, just as other countries try to make their own chips or energy [1][3].
Satellites also guide your phone, your payments and aircraft. Whoever controls them has enormous power, and Europe too is thinking about no longer depending on a single supplier.

news.2026-10-24-coree-du-sud-propose-pou: Seoul proposes that Pyongyang finally mark out the border and restore direct lines
After a North Korean mine exploded on the southern side of the border, Seoul is proposing military talks. A previous appeal went unanswered.

On 23 October, South Korea's Defence Ministry formally proposed military talks to verify together the exact location of the demarcation line, restore military communication lines and avoid accidental clashes [1][2].
Seoul cites a blast on 21 September, in which a South Korean soldier was seriously injured by a North Korean mine laid south of the line; Pyongyang denies it [1][3].

The talks could be held at Panmunjom, possibly with the UN Command. Seoul had already made a similar offer in November 2025, which went unanswered; no reply from the North was known at the time of writing [1][3].
The first sentence to remember: on one of the most heavily armed borders in the world, there is not even agreement on where the line lies [1].
Without direct lines between the armies, a minor incident can become a clash. The local press doubts that the North will accept [2][3].
Lasting tension on the Korean peninsula worries markets and the companies based in South Korea; that is why every attempt at dialogue matters.

news.2026-10-24-etats-unis-budget-defens: The Pentagon asks for $1.5 trillion to catch up with China in drones and AI
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defends the request as a "generational investment" to catch up with China in drones, robotics and artificial intelligence.

Before the Association of the United States Army, Pete Hegseth presented the request of about $1.5 trillion as "critical" so as not to fall behind China in autonomy, robotics and artificial intelligence [1][2].

The breakdown published by a specialist site: $756 billion for new capabilities, $100 billion for air power, $18 billion for the "Golden Dome" missile shield and $10 billion for ships. The Pentagon also plans an autonomous warfare command by October 2027 [1][3].
The budget still has to be passed by Congress. A poll cited by an advocacy group says nearly 60% of Americans consider it too big [4].
The first sentence to remember: Washington is asking for a gigantic sum for its armed forces, and China is named as the reason [1].
Such a budget can push up orders for weapons, drones and chips, and pushes other countries to spend more. Experts nevertheless criticise a budget driven by the amount rather than by a strategy [3].
When Washington spends more on its armies, its allies in Europe are pushed to follow, and that spending is paid for with taxes or debt.

news.2026-10-24-kenya-dangote-oleoduc-ra: Dangote buys a quarter of Kenya's pipeline, ahead of his giant refinery
Africa's richest man is buying nearly 25% of Kenya Pipeline Company for $327 million, a few weeks after the launch of his refinery at Lamu.
Aliko Dangote announced in London on 21 October that he was taking about 25% (24.76% according to a Kenyan newspaper) of Kenya Pipeline Company for 42.5 billion shillings, or $327.4 million [1][2].
The shares come from state-linked investors, including the NSSF social security fund and pension schemes; Dangote did not say which of his companies is buying them [1][2].

The company, 100% state-owned, sold 65% of its capital on the stock market earlier this year. Work on the $16 billion Lamu refinery began on 30 September: 700,000 barrels a day and 1,000 megawatts of electricity [2][3][4].
The first sentence to remember: Dangote wants to control both the refining and the transport of oil in East Africa [1][2].

Kenya is gradually privatising a strategic asset. The Lamu project is meant to eventually produce fuel locally [3][4]. Dangote could get a seat on the pipeline's board and a say in its investments [2].
If Africa refines its own oil, it buys less imported fuel: this can reduce pressure on world prices.

news.2026-10-24-nigeria-ebola-premier-ca: Ebola reaches Abuja: Nigeria confirms its first case and is tracing 44 contacts
A woman who came from Uganda tested positive in Abuja. The outbreak, which started in Congo in May, now reaches West Africa.

On 20 October, Nigeria confirmed in Abuja its first case of the outbreak: a woman who arrived from Uganda, whose symptoms began on 7 October and who has been in isolation since being admitted to a private clinic on 11 October [1][2].

Health Minister Muhammad Pate says he is tracing 44 people who were in contact with her. Uganda replies that it has no confirmed active case and that the woman only passed through on her way from Congo; where she was infected remains to be established [1][2].

The virus involved is the Bundibugyo strain, declared in Congo in May. Kenya has reported nine cases, Africa CDC is holding an extraordinary summit on 28 October, and the WHO speaks of a "complex" outbreak [1][3][4].
The first sentence to remember: the virus has crossed a new border and now reaches the capital of a West African country [2].
When an outbreak spreads, airport checks and travel alerts can slow movement and trade in the region. The WHO advises all neighbouring countries to stay ready [3][4].
The risk for France remains low at this stage, but travellers should follow official recommendations and report any symptoms on returning from an affected area.
